blueprintTopic: Initial corticosteroid for bleeding ITP
scenario: A 33-year-old man comes to the emergency department after two nosebleeds today and blood blisters along the buccal mucosa. He has felt well otherwise and recalls a viral illness three weeks ago. Platelets are 14,000/uL, hemoglobin is 14.1 g/dL, and leukocytes are normal. The smear shows thrombocytopenia with large platelets and no red-cell fragments. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, and he has not received heparin. A CT of the head is not indicated by his normal neurologic examination. He has no procedure scheduled. HIV and hepatitis C results are pending.
question: Which initial therapy is most appropriate?
options: A short course of corticosteroids
Observation and return in one month
Rituximab as the first drug
Urgent splenectomy tonight
Aspirin to improve mucosal circulation
correctAnswer: A short course of corticosteroids
explanation: When an adult with new immune thrombocytopenia has a platelet count below 30,000/uL or mucosal bleeding, initial treatment is a corticosteroid rather than observation. Wet purpura and recurrent epistaxis show that this is more than minor skin bleeding, so waiting a month leaves him exposed to serious hemorrhage. Guidelines favor a short, predefined corticosteroid course, such as oral prednisone with a planned taper or a brief dexamethasone pulse, and advise against months of high-dose steroid. Rituximab is not first-line initial therapy. Splenectomy is reserved for later disease that is steroid-dependent or refractory, after the diagnosis has had time to declare itself and after medical options have been used. Aspirin impairs the remaining platelet function and is harmful here. Intravenous immunoglobulin can be added when a faster rise is required, but the indicated initial class of therapy, with no procedure scheduled in the next hours, is a corticosteroid.

blueprintTopic: IVIG when a rapid platelet rise is required
scenario: A 61-year-old woman with longstanding immune thrombocytopenia is admitted with acute cholecystitis. She is febrile, tender in the right upper quadrant, and needs laparoscopic cholecystectomy, but the surgical service does not want to operate at her current platelet count of 11,000/uL. She has no active bleeding. Hemoglobin is 12.2 g/dL. She is Rh-negative. Steroids were stopped a year ago after a response that took ten days to appear. The gallbladder is inflamed but she is hemodynamically stable, and anesthesia is prepared to proceed once the count is raised.
question: Which platelet-directed therapy best fits the timing of surgery?
options: Intravenous immunoglobulin to raise the count before surgery
Anti-D immune globulin tonight
Splenectomy instead of cholecystectomy
Platelet transfusion as the only ITP treatment
A three-month prednisone taper and delayed surgery despite cholangitis risk
correctAnswer: Intravenous immunoglobulin to raise the count before surgery
explanation: Intravenous immunoglobulin is the guideline-supported way to raise the platelet count quickly when an adult with ITP needs a procedure and there is not time to wait for a corticosteroid response. This patient needs source control of cholecystitis, and her prior steroid response took more than a week. IVIG is therefore the platelet-directed drug that matches the surgical timeline, usually together with a corticosteroid. Anti-D is not an option in an Rh-negative patient and is also avoided when hemolysis would be dangerous. Removing the spleen instead of the gallbladder does not treat the infection and is not how newly urgent ITP is managed. Platelet transfusion alone is rapidly consumed and is not the strategy for a nonbleeding patient who can wait for IVIG to work. Leaving an infected gallbladder untreated for a three-month steroid taper trades a solvable hematologic problem for a surgical one. Once the count is adequate, proceed with cholecystectomy rather than adding an unplanned splenectomy.

blueprintTopic: Life-threatening bleeding in ITP
scenario: A 52-year-old man with known immune thrombocytopenia is brought in after a sudden severe headache and vomiting. He takes no anticoagulant. On arrival he is drowsy but localizes pain. CT shows an acute intracerebral hemorrhage. The platelet count is 6,000/uL, hemoglobin is 12.8 g/dL, INR is 1.0, and the smear has no schistocytes. Neurosurgery is at the bedside. His last ITP treatment was a short steroid course two years ago.
question: Which hematologic treatment is most appropriate in addition to neurosurgical care?
options: Corticosteroid, intravenous immunoglobulin, and platelet transfusion
Observation because the INR is normal
Heparin infusion to prevent clot extension
Aspirin 325 mg once
Splenectomy as the sole immediate measure, without platelets or immunoglobulin
correctAnswer: Corticosteroid, intravenous immunoglobulin, and platelet transfusion
explanation: Life-threatening bleeding in ITP is treated by raising and temporarily replacing platelets, not by watching a normal INR. An intracerebral hemorrhage with a count of 6,000/uL will not stop if the only plan is surgical evacuation while circulating platelets remain in the single thousands. Emergency care combines a corticosteroid, intravenous immunoglobulin, and platelet transfusion so that transfused platelets have a chance to survive while immunotherapy begins to work. A normal INR only excludes a vitamin K-antagonist effect; it does not treat immune platelet destruction. Heparin and aspirin worsen the hemorrhage. Splenectomy can be part of later ITP care, but it does not replace immediate medical therapy in a deteriorating patient and it cannot be the only hematologic intervention before or during emergency neurosurgery. This is also not a disease for antifibrinolytic delay in place of platelet-directed treatment when the count is this low and the bleed is intracranial.

blueprintTopic: Later-line ITP prefers a TPO receptor agonist
scenario: A 49-year-old man was treated for immune thrombocytopenia with a time-limited corticosteroid course four months ago. The count rose, then fell to 12,000/uL within weeks of the taper, and he now has recurrent epistaxis and oral blood blisters. He has required two additional steroid pulses. Hemoglobin and leukocytes remain normal, HIV and hepatitis C tests are negative, and he is tired of insomnia and hyperglycemia on prednisone. A surgeon has offered splenectomy this week as the next and only option. He has no life-threatening bleed today.
question: Which treatment strategy is most appropriate?
options: A thrombopoietin receptor agonist rather than immediate splenectomy
Continuous high-dose prednisone for the next year
Scheduled platelet transfusions twice weekly as maintenance
Aspirin 81 mg daily
Rituximab is forbidden, so surgery must happen this week
correctAnswer: A thrombopoietin receptor agonist rather than immediate splenectomy
explanation: After at least three months of ITP that is corticosteroid-dependent or unresponsive, guidelines suggest a thrombopoietin receptor agonist such as eltrombopag or romiplostim rather than moving directly to splenectomy. This patient has already declared himself steroid-dependent, he is bleeding at 12,000/uL, and he is accumulating steroid toxicity, so simply renewing high-dose prednisone for a year is the strategy the guideline tells clinicians to stop. Splenectomy remains an option for some patients, but it is irreversible, it carries operative and infection risk, and it is not mandatory this week in a patient without life-threatening bleeding who has not been offered a TPO receptor agonist. Maintenance platelet transfusion does not treat the disease and exposes him to alloimmunization and transfusion harm. Aspirin is contraindicated while he is thrombocytopenic and bleeding. Rituximab is another medical option in selected patients; it is not a reason to rush the operating room. The immediate need is a medical second-line plan, not an unplanned splenectomy.

blueprintTopic: HIV and HCV testing in adult ITP
scenario: A 38-year-old man is evaluated for platelets of 22,000/uL found after he noticed petechiae. He feels well, has no fever, and has a normal neurologic examination. Hemoglobin and leukocytes are normal, and the smear shows large platelets without schistocytes or abnormal white cells. He has never been tested for viral infections. He had a short period of injection drug use in his twenties and now has a stable housing situation. The spleen tip is not palpable. No corticosteroid has been started.
question: Which diagnostic test is most appropriate before labeling this primary ITP?
options: HIV and hepatitis C testing
Bone marrow biopsy as a mandatory first test
JAK2 mutation analysis
Heparin-induced platelet antibody assay
Factor VIII activity
correctAnswer: HIV and hepatitis C testing
explanation: Adults who present with a picture of immune thrombocytopenia should be tested for HIV and hepatitis C, because both infections can cause thrombocytopenia and both change treatment and counseling. This history includes prior injection drug use, so the yield of testing is clinically real, but testing is suggested even when the social history is less obvious. The blood count and smear are otherwise typical, so a bone marrow biopsy is not required before making a working diagnosis or starting treatment if bleeding appears. JAK2 testing looks for a myeloproliferative neoplasm, which is not the problem when the only abnormality is thrombocytopenia. A heparin-induced antibody assay is used after recent heparin exposure with thrombosis or a characteristic platelet fall, none of which is present. Factor VIII activity evaluates hemophilia, a coagulation-factor disorder that does not lower the platelet count. Viral testing should not delay a corticosteroid if serious bleeding starts, but in this stable patient it is the indicated diagnostic step.

blueprintTopic: ITP treatment in pregnancy
scenario: A 29-year-old woman at 32 weeks of gestation is found to have platelets of 18,000/uL. She has new gingival bleeding and several oral blood blisters. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, there is no proteinuria, and aminotransferases are normal. Hemoglobin and leukocytes are normal and the smear shows no schistocytes. She had ITP in her twenties that responded to prednisone. The fetus is growing well with a normal tracing. An obstetric colleague recommends cesarean delivery today solely because the platelet count is low.
question: Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Prednisone or intravenous immunoglobulin, with delivery mode based on obstetric indications
Cesarean delivery today solely because of the platelet count
Warfarin to prevent a placental clot
Immediate splenectomy before any medical therapy
Aspirin 162 mg daily until delivery
correctAnswer: Prednisone or intravenous immunoglobulin, with delivery mode based on obstetric indications
explanation: Pregnant patients with ITP who are bleeding or whose platelet count is very low in the third trimester are treated with prednisone or intravenous immunoglobulin, the same classes of therapy used outside pregnancy and chosen because they can be given without the fetal concerns of several other ITP drugs. This patient has mucosal bleeding at 18,000/uL, so observation alone is not enough, and preeclampsia is not the diagnosis: blood pressure, urine protein, and liver enzymes are normal and there are no schistocytes. The route of delivery is decided by obstetric factors, not by ITP itself; a low maternal count is not an indication for immediate cesarean at 32 weeks. Warfarin is teratogenic and causes fetal bleeding and has no role in ITP. Splenectomy is not initial therapy, particularly in the third trimester when medical treatment is available. Aspirin impairs platelet function and is the wrong direction while she is bleeding. Dexamethasone pulses and rituximab are not the pregnancy regimen being chosen here; prednisone or IVIG is.

blueprintTopic: Anti-D is inappropriate in an Rh-negative anemic patient
scenario: A 44-year-old woman with ITP needs a dental extraction in two days. Platelets are 16,000/uL. She is Rh-negative, her spleen is intact, and hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL after a week of menorrhagia. A colleague orders anti-D immune globulin because it is on the hospital ITP pathway for a rapid platelet rise. She is not bleeding from the mouth right now and is hemodynamically stable. Corticosteroids have not yet been restarted.
question: Which choice is most appropriate?
options: Do not give anti-D; use intravenous immunoglobulin for a rapid rise
Give anti-D now because the spleen is still present
Give anti-D and accept an additional drop in hemoglobin
Start aspirin so the extraction will bleed less
Cancel all platelet-raising therapy and extract teeth at 16,000/uL without a plan
correctAnswer: Do not give anti-D; use intravenous immunoglobulin for a rapid rise
explanation: Anti-D can raise the platelet count only in Rh-positive patients who still have a spleen, and it works by causing extravascular hemolysis, so it is avoided in patients who are already anemic or bleeding. This patient is Rh-negative and has a hemoglobin of 8.6 g/dL, so anti-D is the wrong drug twice over: it will not bind her Rh-negative red cells, and further hemolysis is unacceptable. Intravenous immunoglobulin produces a rapid rise without that Rh requirement and is the appropriate choice before a procedure that cannot wait for a slow steroid-only response. An intact spleen does not override the Rh and hemoglobin restrictions. Aspirin increases surgical bleeding. Proceeding with an extraction at 16,000/uL and no plan for a rapid rise ignores the reason the dentist asked for help. A corticosteroid can be started alongside IVIG, but substituting anti-D because it appears on a generic pathway is a preventable hemolytic error.

blueprintTopic: Lower blood pressure before alteplase
scenario: A 68-year-old man with hypertension collapses in a grocery aisle. His wife saw the onset 65 minutes ago. He has aphasia and a dense right hemiparesis. Blood pressure is 206/118 mm Hg and has remained there on repeated measurement. Glucose is 126 mg/dL, platelets are 242,000/uL, and INR is 1.0. He takes amlodipine only. Noncontrast CT shows no hemorrhage and no large established hypodensity. NIHSS is 15. There is no recent surgery, trauma, or bleeding.
question: What is the most appropriate next step in treatment?
options: Lower blood pressure below 185/110 mm Hg, then give intravenous alteplase
Give intravenous alteplase immediately at the current blood pressure
Lower systolic pressure to 110 mm Hg and withhold reperfusion
Start a heparin infusion instead of thrombolysis
Give aspirin and discharge for outpatient MRI
correctAnswer: Lower blood pressure below 185/110 mm Hg, then give intravenous alteplase
explanation: This disabling ischemic stroke is inside the 4.5-hour window, CT shows no hemorrhage, and glucose and coagulation studies do not exclude thrombolysis. Alteplase is not given until blood pressure is below 185/110 mm Hg, and after treatment it is kept below 180/105 mm Hg, because higher pressures raise the risk of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage. A titratable agent such as intravenous labetalol or nicardipine is used, and the pressure is rechecked before the bolus. Giving alteplase at 206/118 mm Hg skips that safety step. Dropping systolic pressure to 110 mm Hg in a pressure-dependent penumbra can enlarge the infarct and is not required; the goal is eligibility, not hypotension. Heparin does not improve outcome in acute ischemic stroke and is not a substitute for reperfusion. Aspirin is the early antithrombotic when thrombolysis is not given, or after 24 hours and a repeat CT when it is given. Once the pressure is controlled, do not withhold alteplase merely because the first reading was high.

blueprintTopic: INR above 1.7 excludes alteplase but not thrombectomy
scenario: A 74-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve and atrial fibrillation takes warfarin. She was speaking normally at breakfast and 50 minutes later could not lift the left arm. Blood pressure is 154/86 mm Hg. Glucose is 108 mg/dL. CT of the head shows no hemorrhage. The stat INR is 2.6. NIHSS is 9. The last warfarin dose was last night. Platelets are 190,000/uL. She has no history of intracranial bleeding.
question: Which acute stroke plan is most appropriate?
options: Withhold alteplase and obtain CT angiography to assess for thrombectomy
Give full-dose alteplase because onset was under an hour
Give half-dose alteplase because of the mechanical valve
Reverse the INR and immediately give alteplase
Start therapeutic heparin as a replacement for reperfusion
correctAnswer: Withhold alteplase and obtain CT angiography to assess for thrombectomy
explanation: An INR above 1.7 is a contraindication to intravenous alteplase, whether or not the patient has a mechanical valve and whether or not the clock time is short. Half-dose alteplase is not a safe workaround for therapeutic anticoagulation. Deliberately reversing warfarin in order to become eligible for alteplase is not the acute ischemic stroke strategy; reversal takes time, leaves the valve temporarily unprotected, and is not how thrombolysis eligibility is created. Therapeutic heparin does not recanalize an acute cerebral occlusion and adds hemorrhage risk. Anticoagulation does not, however, forbid mechanical thrombectomy. If CT angiography shows a large-vessel occlusion and the imaging and clinical criteria for endovascular therapy are met, thrombectomy can still be offered. The correct immediate plan is to withhold the lytic and image the vessels, while the valve team later decides how to resume anticoagulation once the infarct and any hemorrhage risk are defined.

blueprintTopic: Platelets below 100,000 exclude alteplase
scenario: A 59-year-old man with cirrhosis and known thrombocytopenia develops sudden left hemiparesis and neglect while at a clinic visit. Onset was 80 minutes ago. He is alert. Blood pressure is 148/80 mm Hg, glucose is 98 mg/dL, and INR is 1.2. Platelets are 55,000/uL on a sample checked twice. CT shows no hemorrhage and no large hypodensity. NIHSS is 11. He has no ascites leak or active gastrointestinal bleeding today. A resident proposes a platelet transfusion solely to qualify him for alteplase.
question: Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Withhold alteplase and evaluate for large-vessel occlusion thrombectomy
Transfuse platelets and give alteplase as soon as the count exceeds 100,000/uL
Give alteplase now because the INR is normal
Start heparin and aspirin together
Discharge on aspirin without vessel imaging
correctAnswer: Withhold alteplase and evaluate for large-vessel occlusion thrombectomy
explanation: A platelet count below 100,000/uL is a contraindication to intravenous alteplase because the hemorrhagic risk is unacceptable. A normal INR does not cancel that exclusion, and cirrhosis does not create a special lower threshold. Transfusing platelets only to manufacture a number that clears the thrombolysis checklist is not an established, safe eligibility strategy and delays a decision that should already be 'no lytic.' The deficit is still potentially treatable by mechanical thrombectomy if a large-vessel occlusion is present, and thrombocytopenia of this degree does not by itself forbid endovascular therapy the way it forbids alteplase. Dual heparin and aspirin has no role as acute reperfusion. Sending him home on aspirin without vessel imaging misses a time-sensitive occlusion. The immediate actions are to withhold alteplase, obtain noninvasive angiography, and involve endovascular and hematology clinicians for the count, not to chase a laboratory threshold with a transfusion.

blueprintTopic: Wake-up stroke with DWI-FLAIR mismatch
scenario: A 66-year-old man went to sleep at 10 p.m. neurologically well and was found at 7 a.m. unable to speak or move the right side. He is now in a stroke center, 90 minutes after discovery. MRI, already completed, shows a restricted-diffusion lesion that is not yet bright on FLAIR. There is no hemorrhage. NIHSS is 13. Glucose, platelets, and INR are acceptable, and blood pressure is 156/88 mm Hg. He takes no anticoagulant. CT angiography has not yet been done.
question: Which reperfusion decision is most appropriate?
options: Alteplase is reasonable because of DWI-FLAIR mismatch, and vessels should be imaged for thrombectomy
No reperfusion therapy can ever be considered after 4.5 hours from last known well
Heparin infusion for 24 hours, then reassessment
Aspirin alone and no vascular imaging
Alteplase only if FLAIR is already brightly positive
correctAnswer: Alteplase is reasonable because of DWI-FLAIR mismatch, and vessels should be imaged for thrombectomy
explanation: When the time of onset is unknown, a diffusion-positive, FLAIR-negative MRI pattern indicates that the infarct is likely still within the window in which alteplase improves outcome. That mismatch is the imaging selection used for wake-up stroke, so last-known-well time alone does not end the decision. This patient has a disabling deficit, no hemorrhage, and no laboratory exclusion, and the blood pressure is already in range. Alteplase is therefore reasonable. A FLAIR-bright lesion would suggest a more established infarct and would not be the favorable mismatch pattern; the resident has that sign backward. Heparin is not acute reperfusion therapy. Aspirin is what is used when no reperfusion treatment is given, not a reason to skip vascular imaging. CT angiography is still required because a large-vessel occlusion may qualify for thrombectomy on its own imaging criteria even in an extended window. The MRI finding opens the lytic option; it does not replace the search for an endovascular target.

blueprintTopic: Thrombectomy beyond the alteplase window
scenario: A 71-year-old woman had sudden left hemiplegia 8 hours ago. She also had a gastrointestinal bleed requiring transfusion 12 days ago. NIHSS is 18. Blood pressure is 164/90 mm Hg and glucose is 132 mg/dL. Noncontrast CT shows a small core with an ASPECTS score still in the range used for endovascular selection, and CT perfusion shows a small core with a large mismatch meeting trial criteria. CT angiography shows an occlusion of the right M1 segment. There is no hemorrhage.
question: Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Mechanical thrombectomy
Intravenous alteplase despite the clock time and recent bleed
Therapeutic heparin for 48 hours
Comfort care only because 4.5 hours have passed
Intra-arterial thrombolysis on the ward without a catheter team
correctAnswer: Mechanical thrombectomy
explanation: Intravenous alteplase is not appropriate. Onset was 8 hours ago, past the 4.5-hour lytic window, and a gastrointestinal bleed within the prior 21 days is itself a contraindication. Those two facts do not mean reperfusion is over. Selected patients with a large-vessel occlusion and a favorable clinical-imaging mismatch can benefit from mechanical thrombectomy up to 24 hours after onset. This M1 occlusion, severe deficit, small core, and perfusion mismatch are the pattern that extended-window trials used. Heparin does not open an M1 occlusion and is dangerous soon after a major gastrointestinal bleed. Declaring comfort care only because the alteplase clock expired ignores endovascular therapy. Giving a lytic on the ward, intra-arterial or otherwise, without a qualified team and without reversing the reasons alteplase is contraindicated is not a treatment plan. The patient should go to thrombectomy, with the recent bleed communicated to the procedural team so antithrombotic choices during the case are deliberate.

blueprintTopic: No antithrombotic for 24 hours after alteplase
scenario: A 77-year-old man with atrial fibrillation received intravenous alteplase two hours ago for aphasia and right hemiparesis. He is in the intensive care unit, blood pressure is 148/82 mm Hg on labetalol, and the neurologic examination is slightly better. The cardiology consultant wants a heparin infusion started now for the atrial fibrillation and a 325 mg aspirin given with it. Repeat CT has not been done. NIHSS has fallen from 14 to 11. Glucose is 140 mg/dL.
question: Which antithrombotic plan is most appropriate for the next day?
options: Withhold both anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy until 24 hours after alteplase and a repeat CT
Start heparin now and add aspirin tonight
Give aspirin now but wait a week for any anticoagulant
Load warfarin now without bridging or imaging
Start abciximab for 12 hours
correctAnswer: Withhold both anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy until 24 hours after alteplase and a repeat CT
explanation: Antithrombotic drugs are withheld for 24 hours after intravenous alteplase. Aspirin is then considered, classically after a noncontrast CT confirms that there has been no hemorrhagic conversion. Starting heparin two hours after the lytic, especially with aspirin, stacks hemorrhage risk on top of a fresh infarct and does not have an outcome benefit in this setting. Atrial fibrillation will need a later decision about anticoagulation, timed to infarct size and hemorrhagic risk, but that decision is not made by reflex in the first hours. Warfarin loading tonight has the same problem and does not protect against early recurrence anyway. Abciximab and other glycoprotein IIb/IIIa agents are not routine adjuncts to alteplase and increase bleeding. Blood pressure remains under the post-thrombolysis ceiling of 180/105 mm Hg, so the safety issue here is the antithrombotic, not the current pressure. The useful action is to protect the next 24 hours, reimage, and only then choose an antiplatelet or a delayed anticoagulant plan.

blueprintTopic: Correct hypoglycemia before thrombolysis
scenario: A 58-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes is found confused with a right facial droop and right arm weakness. A bystander is unsure of the time but thinks she was normal 30 minutes ago. Capillary glucose is 28 mg/dL. Blood pressure is 150/86 mm Hg. She is diaphoretic. Emergency physicians are about to activate the thrombolysis timer and take her to CT before any medication because the face looks like a stroke. Intravenous access is in place. She has no known head trauma.
question: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Intravenous dextrose, then reassess the neurologic deficit
Intravenous alteplase before the glucose result is addressed
Subcutaneous insulin
Heparin infusion
Discharge as a conversion disorder once the face moves
correctAnswer: Intravenous dextrose, then reassess the neurologic deficit
explanation: Glucose is checked before thrombolysis because hypoglycemia imitates stroke and because alteplase is not given for a metabolic deficit. A value of 28 mg/dL is low enough to explain focal weakness, aphasia, or depressed consciousness, and intravenous dextrose is the specific immediate treatment when intravenous access exists. The examination is repeated after the glucose rises. If a disabling deficit clearly persists and imaging and the rest of the eligibility assessment support ischemic stroke, thrombolysis can still be considered, but it is not the first drug while the patient is profoundly hypoglycemic. Insulin would deepen the hypoglycemia and can cause seizures, arrhythmias, and brain injury. Heparin does not treat either condition. A dramatic improvement after dextrose supports a metabolic mimic and should not be relabeled as a psychiatric conversion disorder without that reassessment; failure to improve after euglycemia puts the team back on the stroke pathway. The dangerous error is to give a lytic, or to do nothing, while a reversible cause is sitting on the glucose meter.

blueprintTopic: Permissive hypertension when thrombolysis is not planned
scenario: A 69-year-old man arrives 12 hours after sudden mild dysarthria that has not progressed. CT angiography shows no large-vessel occlusion and no perfusion mismatch eligible for thrombectomy. Noncontrast CT shows no hemorrhage. NIHSS is 3 and the deficit is nondisabling to mild. Blood pressure is 176/98 mm Hg. Glucose is 118 mg/dL. He takes no anticoagulant. A colleague orders nicardipine to push the systolic pressure to 130 mm Hg before any aspirin is given.
question: Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Give aspirin and do not acutely lower this blood pressure
Lower systolic pressure to 130 mm Hg before any antithrombotic
Give alteplase because the deficit is still present
Start heparin for 24 hours
Withhold aspirin for one week in every ischemic stroke
correctAnswer: Give aspirin and do not acutely lower this blood pressure
explanation: Outside the thrombolysis setting, blood pressure is not routinely lowered unless it is at least 220/120 mm Hg or there is another emergency such as aortic dissection, myocardial infarction, heart failure, or preeclampsia. This reading of 176/98 mm Hg is below that threshold, there is no reperfusion drug that requires a lower ceiling, and forcing it to 130 mm Hg can extend ischemia in a recently symptomatic brain. He is past the alteplase window and has no endovascular target, so a lytic or a thrombectomy activation is not indicated. Aspirin, 162 to 325 mg, is given within 24 to 48 hours after hemorrhage has been excluded, unless a thrombolytic was given in the last day. Heparin is not routine acute therapy for ischemic stroke. Withholding aspirin for a week leaves early recurrence unaddressed in a patient who has no contraindication. Home antihypertensives are restarted thoughtfully after the acute phase, but the emergency department nicardipine order treats a number the guideline does not want treated.

blueprintTopic: Seizure at onset is not an absolute thrombolysis ban
scenario: A 63-year-old man had a witnessed focal seizure that began with right-arm twitching and then a minute of impaired awareness. After the shaking stopped he remained aphasic with a dense right hemiparesis. The seizure started 75 minutes ago and the weakness has not improved. Glucose is 104 mg/dL, blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg, INR is 1.0, and platelets are normal. CT shows no hemorrhage and no tumor. He has no history of epilepsy. The team is told that any seizure at onset permanently forbids alteplase.
question: Which decision is most appropriate?
options: Alteplase is reasonable if the persisting deficit is attributed to stroke
Seizure at onset is an absolute contraindication, so give no reperfusion therapy
Give phenytoin only and repeat the examination in 24 hours before any imaging decision
Start heparin because the event was a seizure
Perform lumbar puncture before CT
correctAnswer: Alteplase is reasonable if the persisting deficit is attributed to stroke
explanation: A seizure at the onset of a focal deficit is not an automatic ban on alteplase. Older rules treated it as one because of fear that the deficit was a Todd paralysis, but current guidance allows thrombolysis when the remaining deficit is thought to be from cerebral ischemia rather than a postictal state and when hemorrhage has been excluded. This man has a persistent, disabling cortical syndrome, a normal glucose, an acceptable blood pressure, no coagulopathy, and a CT without blood or mass. Waiting 24 hours to 'see if it was postictal' forfeits the window if the cause is an occlusion. Heparin is not indicated for either seizure or acute ischemic stroke. Lumbar puncture before CT, in a patient who may have a mass lesion or may need a lytic, is the wrong sequence and adds delay. Antiseizure medication can be given for the seizure itself, but it does not replace the reperfusion decision. Document the reasoning that the deficit is ischemic, and proceed with the stroke pathway rather than an outdated absolute exclusion.

blueprintTopic: Recent intracranial surgery excludes alteplase
scenario: A 70-year-old woman had a craniotomy for a benign meningioma six weeks ago and has been recovering at home. Forty minutes ago she developed left hemiparesis and dysarthria. Blood pressure is 150/84 mm Hg, glucose is 110 mg/dL, and the INR is 1.0. Noncontrast CT shows postoperative changes and no acute hemorrhage. NIHSS is 10. The family asks for 'the clot-busting drug' because they know the time window is short. She is not on anticoagulation. The surgical wound is healed.
question: Which decision about alteplase is most appropriate?
options: Do not give alteplase after intracranial surgery within the past three months
Give alteplase because the CT shows no new hemorrhage
Give alteplase at half dose because the surgery was more than one month ago
Give alteplase after a single dose of heparin
Discharge on aspirin without further stroke evaluation
correctAnswer: Do not give alteplase after intracranial surgery within the past three months
explanation: Intracranial or spinal surgery within the previous three months is a contraindication to intravenous alteplase, as is serious head trauma in that interval. A healed scalp incision and a CT without a new bleed do not remove the risk of catastrophic bleeding into the recent surgical bed. Half-dose alteplase and a heparin primer are not sanctioned ways around that exclusion. The time from onset is short and the deficit is disabling, so the case should still be evaluated for a large-vessel occlusion that might be treated with mechanical thrombectomy, and aspirin can be used if hemorrhage is excluded and no lytic is given. Simply discharging her because thrombolysis is off the table abandons secondary prevention and a possible endovascular option. The specific error to block is equating 'CT negative for blood' with 'safe for a thrombolytic' in a patient whose operation was six weeks ago. Three months is the interval used for this exclusion; six weeks is inside it.

blueprintTopic: ICH blood pressure target
scenario: A 64-year-old man with hypertension is brought from a restaurant after sudden headache, vomiting, and left-sided weakness. Blood pressure is 204/112 mm Hg. CT shows a right basal ganglia hemorrhage about 20 mL with no intraventricular extension and mild local mass effect. He is drowsy but opens his eyes to voice and has a GCS of 13. He takes hydrochlorothiazide only, not an anticoagulant or antiplatelet. Platelets and INR are normal. Neurosurgery does not see an indication for evacuation at this moment.
question: Which blood pressure plan is most appropriate?
options: Lower systolic pressure smoothly toward 140 mm Hg and do not go below 130
Lower systolic pressure to 100 mm Hg as fast as possible
Do not treat blood pressure unless it exceeds 240 mm Hg
Give alteplase once the pressure is lower
Start dexamethasone as the main treatment for the bleed
correctAnswer: Lower systolic pressure smoothly toward 140 mm Hg and do not go below 130
explanation: For spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage of mild to moderate severity with an initial systolic pressure between 150 and 220 mm Hg, acute lowering toward 140 mm Hg, kept in a smooth range of about 130 to 150, is the guideline approach. Pressures below 130 mm Hg and large swings in pressure are associated with harm and are avoided. A target of 100 mm Hg is too low for an acutely injured brain and can produce renal and cerebral ischemia. Leaving a systolic pressure of 204 mm Hg untreated until 240 mm Hg misses the benefit of controlled reduction. Alteplase is a treatment for ischemic stroke and would enlarge this hemorrhage. Corticosteroids do not improve outcome in intracerebral hemorrhage and are not used as disease-modifying therapy. A continuous intravenous agent is preferred so the decline is smooth rather than a stack of precipitous boluses. This deep, moderate-size bleed in a stable patient is managed medically first; the blood pressure plan is the immediate drug decision while neurosurgery remains available if he deteriorates.

blueprintTopic: Reverse warfarin-associated ICH with PCC and vitamin K
scenario: A 79-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation is found down. CT shows a large left intracerebral hemorrhage with early shift. INR is 3.4. Blood pressure is 188/100 mm Hg. He withdraws asymmetrically and does not follow commands. The family reports he took warfarin last night and has not missed doses. Platelets are 210,000/uL. He is not on a direct oral anticoagulant. The pharmacy has both four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate and fresh frozen plasma.
question: Which reversal strategy is most appropriate?
options: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate and intravenous vitamin K
Vitamin K alone
Fresh frozen plasma as the preferred reversal product
Protamine sulfate
Platelet transfusion because the INR is high
correctAnswer: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate and intravenous vitamin K
explanation: Warfarin-associated intracerebral hemorrhage is reversed immediately with four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate and intravenous vitamin K. PCC restores clotting factors faster and with less volume than plasma, which matters in a patient who already has intracranial mass effect. Vitamin K is required as well because factor concentrates are temporary and warfarin will reassert itself without it. Vitamin K alone is too slow for a hemorrhage that is expanding now. Fresh frozen plasma is not the preferred product when four-factor PCC is available; it is slower, it requires blood-type attention, and the volume can worsen pressure. Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin. Platelets do not replace the vitamin K-dependent factors, and the platelet count is normal. Blood pressure is lowered with the same smooth targets used for other intracerebral hemorrhage, but pressure control does not substitute for reversal. Reversal is not delayed for a repeat INR, a swallow study, or a family meeting about goals, although goals of care should be addressed in parallel once the immediate bleed is being treated.

blueprintTopic: Do not transfuse platelets for antiplatelet ICH
scenario: A 72-year-old woman takes aspirin and clopidogrel after coronary stenting six months ago. She has a spontaneous cerebellar-sparing lobar hemorrhage. She is awake, GCS is 14, and neurosurgery plans nonoperative care with close observation. Platelets are 240,000/uL, INR is 1.0, and she has never taken warfarin. Blood pressure is being lowered from 196 to the 140s systolic. A well-meaning order set crosses two units of platelets to 'reverse the aspirin and clopidogrel.'
question: Which hematologic order is most appropriate?
options: Do not transfuse platelets
Transfuse platelets now
Give protamine
Give alteplase after the pressure falls
Start therapeutic enoxaparin tonight
correctAnswer: Do not transfuse platelets
explanation: Platelet transfusion is not recommended for patients with antiplatelet-associated intracerebral hemorrhage who are not undergoing an emergency neurosurgical procedure. A randomized trial found potential harm, and the guideline therefore advises against routine transfusion in this nonoperative setting. The platelet count is already normal; the defect is drug effect on function, and replacing platelets does not translate into better outcomes here. Protamine is the reversal drug for heparin, which she is not taking. Alteplase would be catastrophic in an established hemorrhage. Early therapeutic anticoagulation for the stent is the wrong direction while the bleed is fresh; venous prophylaxis later, after the hematoma is documented to be stable, is a separate decision and is not full-dose enoxaparin tonight. Continue controlled blood-pressure reduction and neurologic checks. If she later needs emergency surgery, the transfusion question can be reconsidered for the operation itself. For the medical management she is actually receiving, cancel the platelet order.

blueprintTopic: Surgical evacuation of deteriorating cerebellar ICH
scenario: A 68-year-old man has a cerebellar hemorrhage. On arrival he was drowsy but protecting his airway. Over the next hour he becomes difficult to arouse, develops pinpoint pupils and extensor posturing, and the repeat CT shows tight posterior fossa mass effect, brainstem compression, and acute hydrocephalus. Blood pressure is being controlled. INR is 1.0. He is not anticoagulated. The intensive care unit has mannitol available and a bed, and a clinician suggests medical management overnight with a plan to 'reimage in the morning.'
question: What is the most appropriate next intervention?
options: Emergency surgical decompression and cerebrospinal fluid diversion
Medical blood-pressure control only until morning
Lumbar puncture to relieve the hydrocephalus
High-dose dexamethasone and observation
Intravenous alteplase
correctAnswer: Emergency surgical decompression and cerebrospinal fluid diversion
explanation: A cerebellar hemorrhage that causes neurologic deterioration, brainstem compression, or hydrocephalus is a surgical emergency. Evacuation of the hematoma and decompression, with ventricular drainage when hydrocephalus is present, can be lifesaving because the posterior fossa has no room for swelling. Waiting overnight on blood-pressure control alone, in a patient who has already moved from drowsy to posturing, is how these patients herniate. Lumbar puncture in a tight posterior fossa can precipitate downward herniation and is not the way to treat obstructive hydrocephalus; an external ventricular drain is placed by the neurosurgical team as part of decompression, with care not to decompress the ventricles in isolation while the cerebellum is still occupying the fossa. Corticosteroids do not treat the mass effect of a hematoma. Alteplase is contraindicated. Blood-pressure management continues, but it is not the definitive intervention once compression and a falling examination are present. Call neurosurgery for immediate operative decompression rather than a morning reimage.

blueprintTopic: No seizure prophylaxis after ICH
scenario: A 60-year-old woman is admitted with a 15 mL cortical hemorrhage. She is alert, talking, and has never had a seizure. The family read that 'bleeds cause seizures' and asks for a preventive antiseizure drug for the next six weeks. Renal function is normal. She is not on an anticoagulant. There is no clinical seizure activity and no history of epilepsy. Blood pressure is at goal.
question: Which medication plan is most appropriate?
options: Do not start a prophylactic antiseizure drug
Phenytoin prophylaxis for six weeks
Carbamazepine prophylaxis for one year
A benzodiazepine infusion for 24 hours despite no seizures
Alteplase once she is comfortable
correctAnswer: Do not start a prophylactic antiseizure drug
explanation: Prophylactic antiseizure medication is not recommended after intracerebral hemorrhage in a patient who has not had a seizure. Trials and the guideline do not show a functional benefit, and some agents, particularly phenytoin, have been associated with worse outcomes. A cortical location raises the later risk of seizures, which is why the family is asking, but risk alone does not justify a preventive prescription. If a clinical seizure occurs, it is treated with an appropriate antiseizure drug, and electrographic seizures in a deteriorating patient are a reason for EEG and treatment. Neither of those has happened. A standing benzodiazepine infusion sedates the examination that nurses are using to detect deterioration. Carbamazepine for a year is an outdated prophylaxis habit, not a guideline strategy. Alteplase has no role. Explain the distinction between prophylaxis and treatment, continue blood-pressure and airway care, and reassess promptly if shaking, a sudden drop in awareness, or an unexplained examination change appears.

blueprintTopic: Idarucizumab for dabigatran-associated ICH
scenario: A 76-year-old man takes dabigatran 150 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation, with the last dose four hours ago. He has sudden headache and left weakness. CT shows an intracerebral hemorrhage. Creatinine clearance is 48 mL/min. He is not on warfarin, aspirin, or a factor Xa inhibitor. Blood pressure is 190/104 mm Hg. The emergency pharmacist asks which specific reversal agent to prepare. Andexanet alfa, idarucizumab, vitamin K, and protamine are all in stock.
question: Which reversal agent is most appropriate?
options: Idarucizumab
Andexanet alfa
Vitamin K
Protamine sulfate
No reversal is needed if blood pressure is lowered
correctAnswer: Idarucizumab
explanation: Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor, and its specific reversal agent is idarucizumab. Intracerebral hemorrhage is an indication to give it promptly rather than to wait and see whether the bleed enlarges. Andexanet alfa is aimed at factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban and rivaroxaban and is not the reversal drug for dabigatran. Vitamin K reverses warfarin by allowing hepatic synthesis of factors and does nothing immediate for dabigatran. Protamine reverses heparin. Blood-pressure control is still required, using the smooth systolic targets for intracerebral hemorrhage, but it does not inactivate circulating anticoagulant. Renal impairment prolongs dabigatran exposure, which is another reason not to rely on time alone four hours after a dose. Four-factor PCC is sometimes discussed when a specific agent is unavailable, but a specific agent is available here and should be used. Give idarucizumab, lower the blood pressure in a controlled way, and avoid antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs. Repeat imaging watches for expansion while supportive care continues.

blueprintTopic: Negative late CT does not exclude subarachnoid hemorrhage
scenario: A 45-year-old woman has a 16-hour history of a headache that began abruptly while she was lifting a suitcase, reached maximum intensity within a minute, and is still severe. She vomited twice and has neck stiffness. She has a history of migraine, but she says this headache is different in onset and intensity. Neurologic examination shows no focal weakness. A high-quality noncontrast CT, read by a neuroradiologist, shows no blood and no mass. She has no bleeding disorder and is not on an anticoagulant. Photophobia is present. A clinician prepares discharge papers for a migraine cocktail.
question: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
options: Lumbar puncture
Discharge with oral sumatriptan
MRI of the brain scheduled next week
Start nimodipine without proving blood
Intravenous alteplase
correctAnswer: Lumbar puncture
explanation: Noncontrast CT is very sensitive for subarachnoid blood in the first hours, but sensitivity falls as blood is cleared and diluted. A negative study 16 hours after a sudden severe headache with meningismus does not exclude aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage. The next diagnostic step is a lumbar puncture, looking for red cells that do not clear between tubes and for xanthochromia. Stopping at the CT is the error this presentation is built to cause, especially when a migraine history offers a comforting alternative. Sumatriptan can worsen vasoconstriction and has no role until bleeding is excluded. Outpatient MRI next week misses a sentinel or active bleed that can rebleed within hours to days. Nimodipine is started after the diagnosis is made, not instead of making it. Alteplase is contraindicated when subarachnoid hemorrhage is the leading concern. If the CT had been performed within about six hours on a modern scanner and read as definitively negative, the conversation about lumbar puncture would be different; at 16 hours that shortcut does not apply.

blueprintTopic: CTA after CT-positive subarachnoid hemorrhage
scenario: A 52-year-old man is brought by ambulance after a sudden collapse and headache at work. He is awake, photophobic, and has neck stiffness. Blood pressure is 168/96 mm Hg. Noncontrast CT shows diffuse subarachnoid blood in the basal cisterns. There is no large intraparenchymal clot and no midline shift. He is not anticoagulated. A trainee asks to perform a lumbar puncture to 'quantify the blood' and another suggests discharge if the headache improves with analgesia. Vessel imaging has not been done.
question: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
options: CT angiography of the head
Lumbar puncture
Discharge if analgesia helps
Carotid duplex ultrasound only
MRI of the cervical spine
correctAnswer: CT angiography of the head
explanation: The CT has already diagnosed subarachnoid hemorrhage, so a lumbar puncture adds pain, delay, and a small risk without changing the immediate plan, and it is especially unwise if a mass effect appears. The next diagnostic question is whether an aneurysm is present and where it is, because rebleeding is the early killer and the aneurysm must be secured. Noninvasive CT angiography is the appropriate next imaging step and catheter angiography is used when needed to plan clipping or coiling. Analgesia may be kind, but improvement with medication does not make an aneurysmal bleed safe for discharge. Carotid duplex does not see the circle of Willis. Cervical spine MRI is not the test for basal cistern blood. While imaging and transfer to a center that can secure the aneurysm are arranged, start oral nimodipine and control blood pressure without causing hypotension. The sequence is CT diagnosis, then vascular imaging, then urgent securing, not a spinal fluid study of a question the CT has answered.

blueprintTopic: Oral nimodipine and urgent aneurysm securing
scenario: A 57-year-old woman has CT-confirmed subarachnoid hemorrhage and CT angiography shows a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm. She is Hunt-Hess grade II, protecting her airway, and blood pressure is 158/92 mm Hg. The neurointerventional team can coil today. No calcium channel blocker has been started. A colleague suggests intravenous nimodipine as a bolus, another suggests 21 days of phenytoin as the drug that improves outcome, and a third suggests bed rest for two weeks before any securing procedure.
question: Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days and urgent securing of the aneurysm
Intravenous nimodipine bolus
Phenytoin for 21 days instead of a calcium channel blocker
Delay securing for two weeks of bed rest only
Heparin infusion to prevent vasospasm
correctAnswer: Oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days and urgent securing of the aneurysm
explanation: Oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days is the pharmacologic intervention shown to improve outcome after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage. It is given by mouth or nasogastric tube, not as an intravenous bolus, because intravenous administration can cause dangerous hypotension and is not the regimen. Nimodipine does not replace securing the aneurysm; early clipping or coiling is what prevents rebleeding, and a two-week delay of bed rest alone leaves the aneurysm exposed during the highest-risk period. Prophylactic phenytoin for 21 days is not the outcome-modifying drug and long courses of antiseizure medication are not routine in patients who have not seized. Heparin does not prevent vasospasm and promotes rebleeding before the aneurysm is secured. Blood pressure is controlled enough to reduce rebleeding risk without hypotension that would compromise perfusion, and definite targets are individualized until the aneurysm is secured. Give the first nimodipine dose now unless the blood pressure will not tolerate it, and move to securing rather than to a prolonged observation admission.

blueprintTopic: Induced hypertension for delayed cerebral ischemia
scenario: A 49-year-old man had his ruptured aneurysm coiled on hospital day 1 and has been receiving nimodipine. On day 7 he develops new aphasia and right-arm weakness over an hour. CT shows no rebleed. CT angiography suggests vasospasm in the left middle cerebral territory. He is euvolemic, sodium is normal, and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. The aneurysm is secured. A team member orders large-volume saline and hemodilution to a low hematocrit, and another suggests nitroprusside to drop the systolic pressure to 90 mm Hg.
question: Which hemodynamic plan is most appropriate?
options: Induced hypertension with a vasopressor while keeping euvolemia
Triple-H therapy with hemodilution and hypervolemia
Lower systolic pressure to 90 mm Hg
Stop nimodipine and start heparin
Alteplase infusion
correctAnswer: Induced hypertension with a vasopressor while keeping euvolemia
explanation: After the aneurysm is secured, symptomatic delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm is treated with induced hypertension on a euvolemic background. The old triple-H package of hypertension, hypervolemia, and hemodilution is not the current strategy: prophylactic or excessive hypervolemia and hemodilution do not improve outcome and cause pulmonary and cerebral edema. This patient is already euvolemic, so the change to make is a careful rise in blood pressure with a vasopressor while neurologic examinations are repeated. Dropping the pressure to 90 mm Hg does the opposite of what an ischemic hemisphere needs. Nimodipine is continued unless it is the cause of limiting hypotension, in which case the dose interval can be adjusted rather than replacing it with heparin. Heparin and alteplase do not treat vasospasm and risk hemorrhage into a recently injured brain. If deficits persist despite induced hypertension, endovascular treatment of the spastic vessel is considered by the neurointerventional team. The bedside error is either over-resuscitating with fluid or treating the blood pressure as if this were a hypertensive emergency.

blueprintTopic: EVD for hydrocephalus after subarachnoid hemorrhage
scenario: A 55-year-old woman is admitted with subarachnoid hemorrhage. Six hours later she becomes progressively less responsive. She was previously opening her eyes to voice and following commands. CT now shows enlarged lateral ventricles and transependymal edema. There is no large temporal hematoma and no new intraparenchymal rebleed. The aneurysm has been identified and securing is planned. Mannitol and a steroid are available. A clinician suggests serial lumbar punctures over the day while waiting to see if she wakes.
question: What is the most appropriate next intervention?
options: External ventricular drainage
Serial lumbar punctures as definitive care
Dexamethasone alone
Heparin infusion
Observation for 72 hours if blood pressure is normal
correctAnswer: External ventricular drainage
explanation: Acute hydrocephalus is a common, treatable cause of decline after subarachnoid hemorrhage. When consciousness falls and CT shows ventriculomegaly, cerebrospinal fluid diversion with an external ventricular drain is the appropriate next intervention, done in coordination with the team that will secure the aneurysm. Waiting 72 hours to see if she wakes accepts preventable herniation and misses the window of a reversible lesion. Serial lumbar punctures are not definitive care for acute obstructive hydrocephalus in this setting and are unsafe if the posterior fossa or a clot is tight. Dexamethasone does not decompress ventricles. Heparin risks rebleeding from an unsecured aneurysm. Mannitol may transiently lower pressure but it does not restore a blocked cerebrospinal fluid pathway. Blood pressure and nimodipine care continue, but the new focal problem on this CT is hydrocephalus, and the matching procedure is a drain. Decline after subarachnoid hemorrhage also prompts a look for rebleeding, seizures, and electrolyte shifts; this scan has already shown the hydrocephalus that explains the examination.

blueprintTopic: Do not puncture after CT has shown subarachnoid blood and mass effect
scenario: A 60-year-old man has sudden headache and a deteriorating examination. CT shows thick subarachnoid blood plus a large temporal lobe hematoma with 8 mm of midline shift. He is obtunded. The on-call clinician wants a lumbar puncture before calling neurosurgery, to 'confirm xanthochromia and relieve pressure.' He is anticoagulated on no agent, INR is 1.0, and blood pressure is 176/100 mm Hg. Pupils are asymmetric. Airway reflexes are still present but the GCS is falling.
question: Which diagnostic decision is most appropriate?
options: Do not perform lumbar puncture; obtain vascular imaging and urgent neurosurgical care
Lumbar puncture immediately to lower intracranial pressure
Discharge if the headache lessens after morphine
Start alteplase for a possible accompanying ischemic stroke
Outpatient MRA in one month
correctAnswer: Do not perform lumbar puncture; obtain vascular imaging and urgent neurosurgical care
explanation: The diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage is already made by CT, and a temporal clot with midline shift and a falling examination is a mass lesion. Lumbar puncture in that setting can precipitate herniation and does not add a result that changes the next hour. It also does not 'relieve pressure' safely when the problem is a hematoma and shift rather than a simple need for spinal fluid removal. The patient needs airway protection as the examination falls, blood-pressure control, nimodipine when enteral access is safe, vascular imaging to find the aneurysm, and urgent neurosurgical and neurointerventional care to evacuate clot if indicated and to secure the aneurysm. Morphine may reduce pain but improvement, or lack of it, is not a discharge criterion. Alteplase is contraindicated with intracranial blood. Outpatient imaging next month is how a sentinel or active aneurysmal bleed rebleeds at home. The tempting extra test is the lumbar puncture; the correct move is to stop it and escalate care.

blueprintTopic: Intravenous lorazepam for convulsive status
scenario: A 40-year-old man is brought from a bus stop after a convulsion that began 8 minutes ago and has not stopped. He has generalized tonic-clonic activity, oxygen saturation of 90% on a nonrebreather mask, and an intravenous line that paramedics placed. Bedside glucose is 102 mg/dL. He has no known trauma. Blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg. A medication list is not available. The team is preparing to roll him for a lumbar puncture before any drug because meningitis is on the differential.
question: What is the most appropriate immediate drug therapy?
options: Intravenous lorazepam
Oral levetiracetam
Intramuscular phenytoin
Succinylcholine without airway control or EEG
No medication until a lumbar puncture is completed
correctAnswer: Intravenous lorazepam
explanation: Convulsive status epilepticus is treated immediately with a benzodiazepine. With intravenous access, intravenous lorazepam is an established first therapy; a typical adult dose is 4 mg, which may be repeated once if seizures continue. Waiting for a medication list, a CT, or a lumbar puncture while the patient is still convulsing extends a time-dependent brain injury. Glucose has already been checked and is normal, so dextrose is not the missing drug. Oral levetiracetam will not be swallowed safely and is not initial abortive therapy. Intramuscular phenytoin is erratically absorbed and is not a benzodiazepine. Succinylcholine can stop the visible movement while seizure activity continues in the brain, and paralysis without a secured airway and EEG hides the very problem being treated. Meningitis may still need evaluation after the convulsion stops, with antibiotics not delayed if the patient is unstable, but the first drug for the ongoing convulsion is lorazepam. Support the airway with positioning and oxygen while the dose is given.

blueprintTopic: Intramuscular midazolam when no IV is available
scenario: Paramedics reach a 36-year-old woman who has been convulsing for 6 minutes in a parking garage. She weighs about 78 kg. There is no intravenous access, and two attempts have failed. Glucose by fingerstick is 96 mg/dL. Oxygen saturation is 88% and improves with a jaw thrust and oxygen. Traffic and positioning make a prolonged on-scene intravenous attempt likely. They carry intramuscular midazolam, intravenous lorazepam that they cannot give, and rectal acetaminophen. The hospital is 15 minutes away.
question: What is the most appropriate immediate medication?
options: Intramuscular midazolam 10 mg
Delay all medication until an intravenous line is placed at the hospital
Rectal acetaminophen
Intramuscular phenytoin
Oral diazepam tablets
correctAnswer: Intramuscular midazolam 10 mg
explanation: When a patient in convulsive status has no intravenous access, intramuscular midazolam is established initial therapy and should not be delayed for further intravenous attempts. In adults heavier than 40 kg the dose used in the evidence supporting this approach is 10 mg. This patient has been convulsing long enough, the fingerstick glucose is not the cause, and a 15-minute deferral of all drugs is a decision to let status continue. Rectal acetaminophen does not stop a seizure. Intramuscular phenytoin is not reliable and is not the first drug. Oral tablets are unsafe in a convulsing patient and too slow. Intravenous lorazepam would be appropriate if a line were already in place, but it is not, and the guideline specifically supports giving intramuscular midazolam rather than losing minutes to access. Airway positioning and oxygen continue during the injection. If seizures persist after adequate benzodiazepine dosing and hospital arrival, a second-line intravenous antiseizure drug is given once access exists. The prehospital error is to transport a cyanotic, convulsing patient with a full vial of midazolam unused.

blueprintTopic: Second-line fosphenytoin after benzodiazepines fail
scenario: A 28-year-old man with epilepsy has received two adequate intravenous doses of lorazepam for generalized convulsions that began 25 minutes ago. He is still convulsing. Glucose is 110 mg/dL. The airway is supported with oxygenation and he is being prepared for intubation if needed. He has no known liver disease, pregnancy, or metabolic contraindication recorded. Home medications are unavailable. A nurse asks whether to give a third and fourth lorazepam as the only plan, or to place oral carbamazepine down a nasogastric tube.
question: Which medication is the most appropriate next antiseizure step?
options: Intravenous fosphenytoin
Repeated lorazepam as the only drug for the next hour
Oral carbamazepine
Cyproheptadine
Dantrolene
correctAnswer: Intravenous fosphenytoin
explanation: After an adequate benzodiazepine dose fails, convulsive status is treated with a second-line intravenous antiseizure drug rather than with an open-ended series of benzodiazepines that deepen respiratory depression without a new mechanism. Intravenous fosphenytoin at 20 mg phenytoin equivalents per kilogram is an accepted next agent. Intravenous levetiracetam or valproate can also be used; they are not listed here because the question asks for one appropriate next drug, and fosphenytoin is appropriate. Oral carbamazepine is too slow and unsafe while he is convulsing. Cyproheptadine is an adjunct for serotonin syndrome, and dantrolene is used for malignant hyperthermia and sometimes neuroleptic malignant syndrome; neither stops status epilepticus as the second-line antiseizure drug. A third benzodiazepine dose is not a substitute for moving to the next phase of treatment. If fosphenytoin and supportive care do not stop the convulsions, the status is refractory and an anesthetic infusion is started with EEG monitoring after the airway is secured. Check glucose once, as was done, and do not delay the second-line drug for a home medication bottle.

blueprintTopic: Anesthetic infusion for refractory status epilepticus
scenario: A 34-year-old woman remains in generalized convulsive status after adequate intravenous lorazepam and a full loading dose of intravenous fosphenytoin. Glucose is 95 mg/dL. She has just been intubated for oxygenation and airway protection. Bedside EEG leads are being placed. Blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg on light sedation from the induction. A proposal is made to extubate once the shaking is chemically paralyzed and to rely on her home oral topiramate alone. Another proposal is dantrolene.
question: What is the most appropriate next seizure-directed therapy?
options: A continuous anesthetic infusion with EEG monitoring
Extubate and give only home oral topiramate
Dantrolene
High-dose aspirin
Observation without further antiseizure medication
correctAnswer: A continuous anesthetic infusion with EEG monitoring
explanation: Convulsive status that continues after a benzodiazepine and a second-line intravenous antiseizure drug is refractory. The next step is a continuous anesthetic infusion, such as midazolam or propofol, titrated with EEG so that electrographic seizures stop rather than only the muscle movement. The airway is already secured, which is a precondition for that sedation, not a reason to extubate. Paralysis without EEG would hide ongoing seizures and is not treatment. Home oral topiramate can be restarted later as maintenance; it will not abort refractory status in a patient who cannot safely receive oral drug as the sole plan. Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia and is sometimes used in neuroleptic malignant syndrome; there is no anesthetic trigger or neuroleptic rigidity syndrome described, and it is not antiepileptic therapy. Aspirin has no role. Stopping at observation after two failed phases accepts ongoing neuronal injury. Vasopressors may be needed because anesthetic infusions lower blood pressure, and that support is part of making the infusion safe rather than a reason to avoid it.

blueprintTopic: Hypoglycemic convulsions need dextrose
scenario: A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is convulsing on the dormitory floor. Roommates say he took insulin and then skipped dinner. The convulsion has lasted several minutes. Fingerstick glucose is 24 mg/dL. An intravenous line is being placed. He has no fever and no head trauma. Someone suggests fosphenytoin as the first drug and someone else suggests insulin because he 'has a diabetes emergency.' Oxygen is applied and he is positioned on his side.
question: What is the most appropriate immediate medication?
options: Intravenous dextrose
Intravenous insulin
Oral phenytoin
Dantrolene
Glucagon by mouth
correctAnswer: Intravenous dextrose
explanation: Hypoglycemia is a reversible cause of seizures and is corrected immediately, before escalating antiseizure drugs as if this were epilepsy. A glucose of 24 mg/dL after insulin without food is sufficient explanation, and intravenous dextrose is the treatment when a line is being placed. If convulsions continue after the glucose is restored, a benzodiazepine is then given as the initial drug for status. Insulin drives glucose lower and can be fatal in this scenario; it treats hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis, not hypoglycemia. Oral phenytoin cannot be safely swallowed during a convulsion and does not raise glucose. Dantrolene does not treat hypoglycemia or status. Oral glucagon is not a formulation or a safe route in an unconscious, convulsing patient; intramuscular or intranasal glucagon is the non-intravenous option when a line cannot be obtained, but intravenous dextrose is preferred once access exists. Do not send him for lumbar puncture or load fosphenytoin while the meter reads 24 mg/dL. Recheck glucose after dextrose and review the insulin dosing so the same omission does not recur tonight.

blueprintTopic: Neurogenic shock after cervical cord injury
scenario: A 27-year-old motorcyclist hits a guardrail and is immobilized on a backboard. CT from the referring hospital shows a C5 fracture. In the trauma bay blood pressure is 78/42 mm Hg and heart rate is 44 beats per minute. Skin is warm and dry. The abdomen is soft, FAST is negative, the pelvis is stable, breath sounds are equal, and there is no external hemorrhage. He cannot move his legs and has weak elbow flexion only. A colleague orders six liters of crystalloid with no vasopressor and another asks for high-dose methylprednisolone as the disease-modifying treatment.
question: Which circulatory plan is most appropriate?
options: Cautious intravenous fluid and a vasopressor for neurogenic shock, with spine immobilization
High-dose methylprednisolone as the primary treatment
Large-volume crystalloid only, with no vasopressor
Sit him upright to treat the bradycardia
Intravenous alteplase for spinal cord infarction
correctAnswer: Cautious intravenous fluid and a vasopressor for neurogenic shock, with spine immobilization
explanation: Hypotension with bradycardia, warm dry skin, and no source of blood loss after a high cervical injury is neurogenic shock from lost sympathetic tone. Treatment is spine immobilization, modest isotonic fluid to fill a dilated vascular bed, and a vasopressor such as norepinephrine to restore vascular tone and support perfusion of the injured cord. Pouring in many liters of crystalloid without a vasopressor causes edema without fixing vasodilation. High-dose methylprednisolone is not recommended for acute traumatic spinal cord injury and adds hyperglycemia and infection without a trauma-course indication. Sitting a patient with a cervical fracture upright is an immobilization failure and can worsen both the cord injury and the blood pressure. Alteplase treats selected ischemic strokes, not traumatic cord compression, and recent major trauma is a bleeding contraindication. This pattern is the opposite of hemorrhagic shock, which is tachycardic and cold until proven otherwise. Keep the collar and log-roll precautions while the vasopressor is started, and recheck for occult bleeding if the picture changes.

blueprintTopic: MRI for cord compression when the patient is stable
scenario: A 54-year-old roofer falls from a low scaffold and has mid-back pain. He can talk and his blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg with heart rate 88 beats per minute. Over six hours in the emergency department his leg strength worsens from antigravity to flicker, a Foley yields 900 mL, and he reports numbness in the saddle distribution. CT shows an L1 burst fracture but does not display the cord or the degree of canal compromise. He has no peritoneal signs and FAST is negative. A clinician suggests high-dose steroids and discharge planning if the CT 'only shows a fracture,' and another suggests immediate flexion-extension bending to test stability.
question: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: MRI of the spine and urgent spine surgery consultation, maintaining precautions
High-dose methylprednisolone and no further imaging
Heparin infusion for presumed cord infarction without imaging
Active flexion-extension stress views now
Discharge with a muscle relaxant
correctAnswer: MRI of the spine and urgent spine surgery consultation, maintaining precautions
explanation: Progressive weakness, urinary retention, and saddle numbness after a burst fracture are cord and cauda equina compression until imaging proves otherwise. CT defines bone but not cord, ligament, or disk. In a hemodynamically stable patient the appropriate next study is MRI, while spinal precautions are maintained and a spine surgeon is called for decompression if the canal is compromised. High-dose corticosteroids are not the treatment of traumatic cord injury and do not replace imaging or surgery. Heparin for a presumed infarct, given before the compressive lesion is seen, risks bleeding into a surgical field and misses the mechanical problem. Flexion-extension testing in a worsening deficit can complete the injury. Discharge on a muscle relaxant ignores a progressive neurologic emergency that is still in a time window where decompression matters. He does not need to bypass resuscitation: his vitals are stable and FAST is negative, which is exactly why MRI, rather than an operating room for hemorrhage, is the right next destination. If he were hypotensive and bleeding, that priority would reverse.

blueprintTopic: Tachycardic hypotension is hemorrhage, not neurogenic shock
scenario: A 41-year-old pedestrian is struck and arrives with a known C6 fracture from an outside CT. Blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg and heart rate is 138 beats per minute. Skin is cool and mottled. The abdomen is distended and tender. Breath sounds are present but the pelvis rocks. He is confused. A transfer note says 'spinal shock, start a vasopressor and skip the blood bank because cord patients are vasodilated.' He has received no blood. Two intravenous lines are in place.
question: Which interpretation and action are most appropriate?
options: Treat hemorrhagic shock with blood and a search for cavitary bleeding
Norepinephrine only, because every cord-injured patient is vasodilated
High-dose methylprednisolone before any fluid
MRI before resuscitation
Oral midodrine and a regular floor bed
correctAnswer: Treat hemorrhagic shock with blood and a search for cavitary bleeding
explanation: Neurogenic shock produces hypotension with bradycardia and warm skin because sympathetic drive is lost. This patient is tachycardic, cool, and has a distended tender abdomen plus an unstable pelvis, which is hemorrhagic shock until proven otherwise. A cervical fracture does not explain the heart rate and does not allow the team to skip blood. Damage-control resuscitation uses blood products early rather than vasopressors alone or crystalloid in unlimited volume, and the bleeding compartments are addressed: pelvis binding if the pelvis is the source, chest and FAST or operative control for the abdomen, and an airway as mental status falls. MRI while hypotensive and tachycardic removes a bleeding patient from resuscitation. Steroids do not restore volume. Oral midodrine is an outpatient orthostatic drug, not trauma care. Vasopressors may be added after hemorrhage is controlled and volume is restored, but leading with them while the abdomen is full of blood worsens tissue perfusion and hides the source. The cervical collar stays on, but the circulation problem is bleeding.

blueprintTopic: Bronchiolitis supportive care instead of bronchodilators
scenario: A 7-month-old, born at term, has had rhinorrhea and a worsening cough for three days. An older sibling is home with a cold. The infant is wheezing with scattered crackles, respiratory rate 62, oxygen saturation 86% on room air, and mild subcostal retractions. Temperature is 38.0 C. He still has wet diapers and a moist mouth. There is no focal consolidation suspected on examination, no apnea, and he is alert. The family asthma history is limited to an uncle. A nebulizer and a dexamethasone dose are drawn because 'this is how the cousin's asthma is treated.'
question: Which treatment plan is most appropriate?
options: Supplemental oxygen, nasal suction, and hydration assessment, without bronchodilators or corticosteroids
Scheduled albuterol and oral dexamethasone
Azithromycin for five days
Chest physiotherapy every hour
Ceftriaxone because any fever means bacterial pneumonia
correctAnswer: Supplemental oxygen, nasal suction, and hydration assessment, without bronchodilators or corticosteroids
explanation: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis, and the therapies that feel like asthma care do not help. Supplemental oxygen is appropriate when saturation is persistently below 90%; this infant is at 86%. Nasal suction, especially before feeds, relieves obstruction, and hydration is supported by mouth if possible. Albuterol and epinephrine are not recommended, and a family history of asthma does not convert viral bronchiolitis into a steroid-responsive asthma attack. Systemic corticosteroids are not indicated. Antibiotics are not given unless there is a concomitant bacterial infection, which a low-grade fever and diffuse wheeze do not establish. Chest physiotherapy does not change the course. A routine chest radiograph often leads to unnecessary antibiotics and is not required when the diagnosis is clinically clear. The dangerous distraction is the nebulizer already drawn up. Give oxygen, suction, and observe the work of breathing and feeding rather than stacking asthma drugs.

blueprintTopic: Mild bronchiolitis does not need a bronchodilator trial
scenario: A 5-month-old arrives at an urgent care clinic on day 2 of nasal congestion and cough. Respiratory rate is 48, oxygen saturation is 95% while awake, and retractions are minimal. He is taking bottles and has normal urine output. Lungs have wheezes and crackles but good air movement. Temperature is 37.8 C. The parent asks for the breathing treatment and steroid shot that a relative received for asthma last winter. The clinician wonders whether one albuterol trial is required before discharge teaching.
question: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Supportive care and discharge teaching without albuterol or corticosteroids
A mandatory albuterol trial before any discharge
Oral dexamethasone for three days
Chest radiograph and azithromycin
Continuous pulse oximetry at home for one week
correctAnswer: Supportive care and discharge teaching without albuterol or corticosteroids
explanation: This infant has mild bronchiolitis: he is hydrated, saturations are above 90%, and work of breathing is modest. The guideline recommends against albuterol and against systemic corticosteroids, including a 'trial' that tends to be continued if anyone hears less wheeze for a few minutes. Discharge teaching covers nasal suction, feeding, return precautions for apnea, poor feeding, or increased work of breathing, and avoidance of tobacco smoke. A chest radiograph and an antibiotic treat a bacterial diagnosis he does not have. Home continuous oximetry is not required for a mild, non-hypoxic infant and often generates false alarms. Fever at this level with a typical viral examination does not trigger ceftriaxone. The age, 5 months, is squarely inside the bronchiolitis guidance and is not the neonatal sepsis band, so the absence of toxic appearance matters. Send him home with supportive care rather than an asthma protocol borrowed from an adult relative.

blueprintTopic: No routine radiograph or antibiotics in bronchiolitis
scenario: An 11-month-old is on hospital day 2 for bronchiolitis. He is on 0.5 L of oxygen with saturations of 93%, taking some feeds, and afebrile now. The admission examination showed diffuse wheeze without a focal finding. Viral testing was not sent. On rounds a consultant orders a daily chest radiograph, a full viral panel, and ceftriaxone 'because RSV becomes pneumonia.' The nurse reports no apnea and a reassuring capillary refill. White count has not been drawn.
question: Which modification to the orders is most appropriate?
options: Cancel the routine radiograph, viral panel, and ceftriaxone, and continue supportive care
Add scheduled albuterol to the ceftriaxone
Add dexamethasone and chest physiotherapy
Obtain the radiograph and start antibiotics if any perihilar markings are seen
Discharge today off oxygen because hospital day 2 is an automatic endpoint
correctAnswer: Cancel the routine radiograph, viral panel, and ceftriaxone, and continue supportive care
explanation: Routine radiographs and laboratory studies, including viral panels, are not recommended in bronchiolitis when the clinical diagnosis is clear. They rarely change management and radiographs of viral lung disease are often read as pneumonia, which pulls in antibiotics the guideline says not to use unless a separate bacterial infection is present. This child is afebrile, diffusely wheezy, and improving on oxygen, so ceftriaxone is not treating a defined bacterial focus. Albuterol, dexamethasone, and chest physiotherapy remain unhelpful add-ons. He does still need oxygen and observation; an arbitrary discharge on day 2 while he requires oxygen is not the supportive plan.
